
### fragmentation  {.smaller}



* max frame data size on my local network = 1500 bytes, but…
 
```
$ ping6 fe80::da07:b6ff:fed9:ae50 -s 4000
PING fe80::da07:b6ff:fed9:ae50 (fe80::da07:b6ff:fed9:ae50) 4000 data bytes
4008 bytes from fe80::da07:b6ff:fed9:ae50%eno1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.17 ms
4008 bytes from fe80::da07:b6ff:fed9:ae50%eno1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.779 ms
4008 bytes from fe80::da07:b6ff:fed9:ae50%eno1: icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=0.742 ms
...
$ ping -s 4000 192.168.1.1                 
PING 192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1) 4000(4028) bytes of data.     
4008 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.891 ms 
4008 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.806 ms 
4008 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=0.748 ms 

```


### fragmentation  {.smaller}


* original sender or router splits packet into multiple
* each part called a <i>fragment</i> 
<hr class="vspace" />
* stored temporarily and ‘‘reassembled’’ at receiver 

   * Linux defaults: <br> max 64 packet gap between fragments per source IP <br> 30 second time limit before discaded <br> 3-4MB buffer of packets



### IPv6 fragments 


![](/routing-intro/ipv6-fragment-ex){fig-alt="Wireshark screenshot of the ping6 command from an earlier slide. There are groups of three packets, which wireshark identifies as two IPv6 fragments followed by an ping request or reply. The packet that wireshark identifies as the ping request/reply is actually the third fragment of the original IPv6 packet, which wireshark hsa rconstructed. Details for one middle fragment is shown. The IPv6 next header type is 'fragment header for IPv6', and the fragment header has an offset, a more fragments field, and a packet idenitfier."}


### IPv4 fragments 


![](/routing-intro/ipv4-fragment-ex){fig-akt="Wireshark screenshot of the ping command from an earlier slide. There are groups of three packets, identified as a fragments followed by a ping request/reply like before. Unlike IPv6, the fragment information is part of fields of the IP header itself, which includes a more fragments field, a fragment offset, and a packet identification."}


### varying frame size support  {.smaller}


* also called <i>maximum transmission unit</i> (MTU) 
<hr class="vspace" />
* typical Ethernet, Wifi --- 1500 bytes
* Ethernet with ‘‘jumbo frames’’ -- 65535 bytes
* IPsec ESP VPN over 1500-byte MTU network -- $\sim$ 1400--1440 bytes 

   * VPN --- simulated network link over other network links



### routers making fragments  {.smaller}


* option in IPv4 to handle frame size mismatch, but not great: 
<hr class="vspace" />
* extra data sent over network (especially if just over max size) 

   * extra copies of main headers on each fragment

* extra work at receiver to reconstruct fragments
* lose whole packet if one fragment is lost 

   * but other routers likely to still waste time forwarding all other fragments



### avoiding fragmentation  {.smaller}


* IPv4 --- DF (don't fragment) flag in packets 

   * if set, routers not allowed to fragment packet

* IPv6 --- routers never fragment packets 

   * any fragments made at source machine only
 
<hr class="vspace" />
* when set --- ICMP error 

   * ICMPv6: Packet Too Big
   * ICMPv4: destination unreachable + reason code of fragmentation needed
   * (hopefully, bad networks might drop packet instead)

* ICMPv6 error tells you maximum supported size 

   * (by first link that got packet rejected --- might be more constraining link later)
   * info not available in IPv4
